target_claim: Solution 5's selection rule (lines 0009-0011): after deleting e from T1 to get components A,B, 'there must exist at least one edge f in T2 that connects a vertex in A to a vertex in B. Choose any such edge f' -- and then (line 0027) 'Therefore (V, (T2 \ {f}) u {e}) is a tree.' The claim under test is that ANY T2-edge crossing the cut (A,B) makes (V,(T2\{f}) u {e}) a tree.
failing_input: n=4, V={1,2,3,4}. T1 = {1-2, 1-3, 1-4} (star at 1), T2 = {1-2, 2-3, 3-4} (path 1-2-3-4), e = {1,3} in T1. Deleting e from T1 gives A={1,2,4}, B={3}. The T2-edges crossing (A,B) are {2-3} and {3-4}; the solution's step 2 permits either. Take f = {3,4}: (T2\{f}) u {e} = {1-2, 1-3, 2-3}. Second (deterministic-reading) instance where even the FIRST crossing edge in canonical sorted order fails: T1 = {1-2,1-3,1-4}, T2 = {1-3,2-4,3-4}, e = {1,4}, A={1,2,3}, B={4}, first crossing edge f = {2,4}, giving (T2\{f}) u {e} = {1-3,1-4,3-4}. Triage's own sketch instance also reproduces: T1={1-2,2-3,3-4}, T2={1-2,1-3,1-4}, e={2,3}, f={1,4} -> {1-2,1-3,2-3}.
observed_vs_claimed: Solution asserts (line 0027) that (V,(T2\{f}) u {e}) is a tree for any crossing f. Oracle is_tree (|E| = n-1 AND BFS-connected AND union-find-acyclic; exact integer/set arithmetic, no floats) says FALSE on the failing input: {1-2, 1-3, 2-3} on V={1,2,3,4} is the triangle 1-2-3 with vertex 4 isolated -- it has 3 = n-1 edges but is both cyclic and disconnected. The first exchange (T1\{e}) u {f} = {1-2, 1-4, 3-4} IS a tree, so only the second half of the solution's verification (step 4) is refuted. Scale of the defect, from the exhaustive sweep over ALL ordered pairs of labelled trees: n=3, 6/9 pairs admit a bad (e,f); n=4, 240/256 pairs, 456 bad (e,f) choices of which 204 are the FIRST crossing edge in canonical order; n=5, 15500/15625 pairs, 51180 bad choices of which 20662 first-in-order. Seeded random sweep (seed=20260820, 400 pairs per size) at n=6..12: 400/400 pairs bad at every size, with 2042 (n=6) up to 8910 (n=12) bad (e,f) choices per batch. The underlying THEOREM is verified true throughout (for every (T1,T2,e) tested, some valid f always exists -- asserted in the run), so the defect is exactly the solution's selection rule, not the problem statement.
faithfulness_notes: The solution's procedure is fully implementable as written and was implemented literally. Step 1 ('removing e from T1 disconnects the graph into exactly two components A and B') is `components_after_removing`, a BFS on T1\{e} from e[0]; A is that component, B its complement. Step 2 ('there must exist at least one edge f in T2 that connects a vertex in A to a vertex in B; choose any such edge f') is `crossing_edges`, which returns ALL such candidates in canonical sorted order. Because the text says 'choose any', the solution's step-4 assertion is universally quantified over that choice, so the search tests BOTH readings: (a) the deterministic reading f := the first candidate in canonical sorted order, and (b) the universal reading, every candidate. Both readings are refuted, and the counterexamples reported are the smallest NON-DEGENERATE ones (e not already an edge of T2, so no set-union collapse); degenerate n=3 failures with e in T2 also exist but were deliberately not used as the headline. (T1\{e}) u {f} and (T2\{f}) u {e} are formed as set difference/union exactly as the problem writes them, so results are simple graphs, not multigraphs. Tree enumeration uses an unambiguous O(n^2) Prufer decoder giving all n^(n-2) labelled trees; the oracle was self-tested on five hand-checked cases before use. Everything is exact int/set arithmetic; no floating point and no wall-clock anywhere. Root cause of the bug: the solution needs f to lie on the unique u-v path in T2 (equivalently, on the unique cycle created by adding e to T2), which is strictly stronger than merely crossing the cut (A,B) whenever that path crosses the cut more than once; line 0026's justification ('e was the unique edge in T1 connecting A and B') is a true statement about T1 that is irrelevant to whether T2\{f} plus e is connected.
